https://bnn-news.com/former-sputnik-empl.text: Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Home Baltics Baltics Social Former Sputnik employee: “Baltic Antifascists” is a Russian Intelligence Services project LETA August 31, 2026 Facebook Twitter Marats Kasems, former editor-in-chief of Sputnik Lithuania Photo: Lita Millere/LETA The “Baltic Antifascists” project was created by Russian intelligence services, Marats Kasems, former editor-in-chief of Sputnik Lithuania, claimed in an interview on the LETA podcast “Kas tas vispār bija?! Aiz priekškara” (“What Was That?! Behind the Curtain”). Kasems said that Telegram channels funded from Russia’s propaganda budget should be distinguished from “Baltic Antifascists”, which he described as a “pure intelligence services project”. According to Kasems, the project was created at the request of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). He claimed that the project’s leader has publicly spoken about preparing reports for intelligence services and compiling lists of people considered disloyal to Russia so that, in the event of a potential occupation, these people could be “eliminated”. Kasems acknowledged that he does not possess any public documents proving these alleged links. He said that he himself had been offered a position as an expert for the project but declined after learning about its possible ties to Russian intelligence services. According to him, the project initially also considered producing content in Latvian, Lithuanian and Estonian. LETA has not independently verified Kasems’ claims regarding the project’s alleged links to Russian intelligence services. Latvia’s State Security Service (VDD) has identified various activities on the “Baltic Antifascists” Telegram channel that are directed against Latvia’s national security interests. The channel consistently glorifies Russia, its political regime and foreign policy, as well as its aggression against Ukraine. It has published calls to carry out cyberattacks against Latvian government institutions and private-sector companies. Followers of the channel have also been encouraged to collect information about the infrastructure of the Latvian National Armed Forces and NATO allied forces in Latvia. The channel also compiles information about Latvian state officials and other prominent public figures who, through their political and public activities, oppose Russia’s war against Ukraine. According to claims made on the channel, the information is intended to be passed on to Russian intelligence services and other institutions so that various measures can be taken against these individuals. According to the VDD, the main objective of these activities is to influence public opinion and decision-making processes in Latvia in line with Russia’s interests by exerting psychological pressure on Latvian officials and society. As previously reported, Latvian prosecutors imposed a EUR 15,500 fine on Kasems for assisting Russia in activities directed against Latvia. He admitted his guilt and paid the fine. Kasems was initially detained in criminal proceedings concerning a suspected violation of EU sanctions, but the case was later reclassified as assistance to a foreign state in activities directed against Latvia. Between 2017 and November 2022, the Latvian citizen provided intellectual and practical support to Russia for personal reasons and financial gain. The accused was aware that one of Russia’s objectives was to strengthen and expand its influence in the Baltic States and other European Union countries, including through activities directed against Latvia’s national independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, state authority, constitutional order and national security as a whole. The accused fully accepted the scope and legal classification of the criminal offence with which he was charged, admitted his guilt and expressed remorse. Following the ruling, a public debate emerged over whether the punishment imposed on Kasems, a pro-Kremlin activist and editor of the Russian media outlet Sputnik Lithuania, was adequate. After the prosecutor’s decision was made public, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs stated that “several recent decisions by the Prosecutor’s Office raise a number of questions”. The Judicial Council subsequently announced that it would review the existing sentencing policy in corruption and national security cases. https://www.dw.com/en/starlink-how-elon-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/58jZN Starlink satellites have become vital means of communication in war zones Image: Depositphotos/IMAGO Advertisement Lack of internet access is a major problem in many regions of the world today. Starlink was initially developed by the American tech billionaire Elon Musk to solve this problem. It was designed as a way of quickly getting the internet into regions all over the world where this was either impossible to do by conventional methods, or so expensive that it wasn't worth attempting. Starlink and SpaceX founder, controversial billionaire Elon Musk Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Since then, Starlink's field of application has widened significantly. It's used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments. But there is a downside: Ukraine's military, for example, is heavily dependent on Musk's satellite system. This has become especially apparent as the service faces external disruption. How does Starlink work? Starlink, which is operated by Musk's SpaceX company, is a satellite-based system consisting of 10,000 small satellites located around the world. They transfer data packages via laser links and do not require a constant, direct visual link to a ground station. Unlike other internet satellites, which orbit at around 36,000 kilometers (22,000 miles) above the Earth, Starlink satellites are only about 550 kilometers up. This means they can transmit internet signals much faster than the others. All users need is a small receiver terminal with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically steers toward the satellites as they pass overhead. The terminals receive signals from these satellites and transmit them to a nearby router, which supplies the broadband internet connection. Starlink receivers smuggled into Iran enabled the opposition to organize despite the internet shutdown Image: Middle East Images/picture alliance Where has Starlink already been deployed? Ukraine: Since the start of the Russia's full-scale war in February 2022, Starlink has become a vital instrument of communication in the war zone. The Ukrainian armed forces use Starlink to coordinate units, operate drones and control unmanned ground systems. In the civilian sector, the system is used by hospitals, emergency services, energy suppliers and the railway network. Ukraine offers a particularly vivid example of how heavily its military capabilities now depend on Starlink. In mid-October, Ukrainian army units reported disruptions to data transmission, which are said to have severely affected the control of combat, interceptor- and reconnaissance drones. Elon Musk said that restrictions on the speed and use of Starlink are determined by the US military and ultimately the US president. At this stage, it remains unclear who ordered the restrictions. Iran: In early January 2026, protests erupted all across the country against the regime in Tehran. The government's hardline response included a nationwide internet shutdown . Reportedly, thousands of Starlink terminals were smuggled into Iran and sold on the black market. This enabled the protest movement to go on coordinating demonstrations against the regime, using Starlink to circumvent state censorship of the internet. How reliable is Starlink as a wartime communications line? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The country's authorities are cracking down on the satellite service and its users. Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace, described Starlink as a hostile "tool of war" and said the regime had means at its disposal to disrupt satellite connections. Starlink is officially banned in Iran. Anyone using the service faces a prison sentence of six months to two years. If users are also charged with endangering national security or espionage, the offence can even carry the death penalty. Sudan: In the Sudanese civil war, Starlink is used primarily by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group fighting against the internationally-recognized government. Hundreds of devices were smuggled into the country via the United Arab Emirates, and there is now a thriving black market for Starlink terminals in Sudan . The RSF use them to communicate and coordinate with their militias, while the Sudanese Armed Forces are trying to block both the import and use of the terminals. Venezuela: Here too, Starlink has been used in the past to sidestep information blackouts and secure access to the internet. For a long time, the service was only available unofficially, by buying kits from local dealers. Following the US intervention in early January 2026, during which then-head of state, Nicolas Maduro , was taken prisoner, Musk offered the people of Venezuela a month's free broadband internet service via Starlink. Gaza: Starlink has been used for humanitarian purposes in the devastated Gaza Strip since July 2024. Aid organizations and a field hospital use it to facilitate telemedical assistance and logistical coordination. Access for civilians remains limited because of Israeli security concerns. Why has Starlink been criticized? Starlink is often the only way to access the internet in conflict zones. This gives Musk and his operating company SpaceX tremendous influence. Previously, for example, Musk refused to activate Starlink in Ukraine to enable an attack in Crimea . US President Donald Trump has also threatened to switch off the satellites in Ukraine, as a way of forcing Kyiv to make concessions in peace negotiations. Starlink has provided vital communications for Ukrainian soldiers since the start of the 2022 Russian invasion Image: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance There has also been criticism from an ecological perspective. The Starlink satellites have a lifespan of less than five years. Every day, on average, one or two of them burn up in the Earth's atmosphere. This releases aluminum oxide, which could affect the ozone layer, contributing to global warming. In addition, all those thousands of satellites reflect the sunlight, making the night sky brighter , and this may also have repercussions for the world's animals. Any Starlink alternatives? In an effort to break Starlink's monopoly, other companies, especially in Europe, are already working on alternatives. At present, the biggest private competitor to SpaceX is a company called Eutelsat. With a fleet of over 600 satellites, its OneWeb service is far smaller, focusing on business customers and maritime use. But Eutelsat is also involved in the development of IRIS2 — an acronym for Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite, an ambitious EU project to establish a highly secure satellite network. The aim is to make Europe less dependent on Starlink , but IRIS2 won't be fully operational before 2032. Elon Musk also has competition inside the US from another billionaire, Jeff Bezos, whose company Amazon is currently working on Amazon Leo, known until recently as Project Kuiper. This is establishing a network of more than 3,200 new low-Earth-orbit satellites. Amazon plans to roll out the service later this year in the US, Canada, France, Britain and Germany. Chinese competition for Starlink and SpaceX: The launch of a Chinese rocket carrying astronauts to a space station in April 2025 Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance The sky is clearly getting crowded . China is also refining two satellite communications systems of its own. Guowang, a state project conceived primarily for national and military purposes, will consist of up to 13,000 satellites, while another project, Qianfan, with an estimated 12,000 satellites, is more commercially oriented and aims to provide services to newly industrialized and developing countries. The first mass starts for both of these projects are planned for this year. Will Russia have its own Starlink? From Emmanuel Macron's France to Edi Rama's Albania , the student and pupil mobilizations of October 2026 have evolved into much more than a protest over education . Behind the clashes emerges a deeper crisis of trust in the political system, at a time when upcoming electoral contests acquire special significance. From school classrooms to the streets — How the explosion started The image forming in Europe over recent weeks causes intense concern. Thousands of pupils and students are abandoning classrooms, organizing mobilizations, and clashing with government policies, denouncing that the educational system no longer offers them the opportunities they were promised. In France, the protest wave began from daily school life problems: teacher shortages, overcrowded classes, facilities needing repairs, and uncertainty regarding access to higher education. In Albania, discontent over study costs and limited career prospects combined with broader allegations of corruption and challenges to the government. Despite differing conditions, there is a common denominator: young people who feel that political decisions determine their future without seriously considering their needs. France: Over 1,000 schools in mobilizations — The crisis escapes educational bounds France sits at the epicenter of the new student unrest. Mobilizations began in late September, starting from the Saint-Exupéry high school in the Créteil area near Paris. Within days they spread to different regions of the country. On October 1, a decisive turning point occurred: according to Le Monde , more than 1,000 schools, nearly a quarter of the total, participated in the mobilizations. Students demanded more educators, better infrastructure, and substantive changes in the school environment. However, as protests expanded, their character changed as well. In several areas, school blockages were accompanied by clashes with police forces . Trash bins were set on fire, objects were hurled, and police used riot control means. Educators and school principals expressed concern that the situation was beginning to spin out of control, while acknowledging that many student demands were justified. Tear gas, arrests, and injuries — Police response provokes fresh rage Images from the French demonstrations opened a second, exceptionally sensitive front: the treatment of underage protesters. According to an Associated Press report on October 16, thousands of demonstrators, mostly under 18 years of age, have been arrested during the mobilization wave. Severe teenager injuries and allegations of excessive police force have also been recorded. On the other side, French police report over 900 injured officers and 150 school staff members, maintaining that violent groups exploit mobilizations for attacks and destruction. The confrontation no longer limits itself to whether students have a right to protest. It also concerns the proportionality of police intervention, the protection of minors, and the authorities' responsibility to prevent violence. For Emmanuel Macron, the crisis is evolving into yet another difficult test during the final months of his presidency. France possesses a long tradition of social mobilizations, but the participation of such a large number of students imparts special political weight to current unrest. The 2027 budget and accumulated discontent The explosion of student rage cannot be decoupled from broader fiscal pressures in France. Student mobilizations coincided with public sector strikes and intense reactions against government budget proposals. On October 13, as parliamentary debate for the 2027 budget commenced, students and unions demonstrated again. Although the government proposal includes a €1.2 billion increase for the Ministry of Education, educational organizations consider that measures do not adequately address accumulated problems. Characteristically, out of 3,000 substitute teachers announced for priority schools, only 35% of the target had been achieved by October 13, according to Education Minister Édouard Geffray. This explains why government announcements have so far failed to restore trust. Students do not solely demand larger funds; they demand to see immediate changes in their daily lives. Albania: From the "flamingo revolution" to the fires of Tirana If in France the crisis started from school classrooms, in Albania the explosion of youth discontent possesses even deeper political and economic roots. Violent mobilizations in October did not appear suddenly. The so-called "flamingo revolution" began on May 30, 2026, prompted by a controversial tourism development plan near Zvërnec and the Vjosa wetlands. The construction of a luxury tourist complex in an ecologically sensitive area provoked reactions for natural environment protection, while the project linked to business interests including Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. The movement soon surpassed its environmental demands. Protesters began denouncing corruption, the influence of powerful business interests, social inequalities, and the economic model of Edi Rama's government. According to an analysis by the Polish Center for Eastern Studies (OSW), mobilizations also express discontent over mass youth emigration, limited career prospects, and distrust toward the entire political elite. Three days of violent clashes — Fires in public buildings and banks From October 13 to 15 (continuing into 10/16), Tirana transformed into the epicenter of severe clashes. Thousands of protesters, among them high school and university students, held marches demanding educational reforms and, in many cases, the resignation of Edi Rama. Mobilizations evolved into violent conflicts when groups of protesters attacked police cordons and government buildings. Fires were recorded in governmental facilities and bank branches, destruction of businesses, hurling of stones and fireworks, as well as police interventions with tear gas and water cannons. The Associated Press reported that 71 police officers were injured during incidents, alongside protester injuries and arrests. The Albanian government condemned destruction and accused political opponents of inciting violence. Conversely, mobilization organizers maintain that protests result from months of indifference toward their demands. The European Union delegation in Albania expressed concern over escalation and requested a proportionate response from authorities. Why rage in Albania targets the entire political system The Albanian case presents a particularly interesting difference from the French one. In France, the core of protests remains closely tied to public schooling, despite gradual politicization. In Albania, educational discontent integrated into an already shaped anti-government movement . Students denounce high study costs, inadequate financial support, and difficulties finding employment after graduation. Behind these demands lies a broader anxiety: that even acquiring a university degree does not ensure a decent professional and economic prospect. Concurrently, protest does not restrict itself exclusively to the government. Certain participants express distrust toward the traditional opposition as well, considering that previous decades' power alternations failed to address the country's structural problems. This explains why the movement struggles to fit into a simple government-opposition confrontation scheme. Belgium and Italy: Protests cross borders The picture is not confined to France and Albania. In October, student and pupil mobilizations were also recorded in Belgium and Italy. In Belgium, incidents in Liège were accompanied by arrests and temporary school closures. In Italy, students participated in demonstrations across various cities, though mobilization scale was smaller than France's and demands connected more closely to specific domestic conditions. It is therefore not substantiated that all of Europe faces a single unified uprising. However, parallel outbursts of youth discontent present common characteristics: anxiety about the future, distrust toward institutions, and a sense that political leaderships fail to respond to the new generation's needs. In Greece University students gathered outside the Ministry of Finance in Athens on Tuesday to protest rent hikes and the lack of affordable student housing. Scenes set at Syntagma Square near parliament during a protest in Athens. The major political dimension: The 2027 French elections The temporal juncture of demonstrations is exceptionally important. France approaches the 2027 presidential elections , in which Emmanuel Macron cannot claim a third consecutive term. Thus, mobilizations evolve into a core issue of pre-electoral confrontation. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, head of La France Insoumise, has sided with student demands, denouncing police handling of demonstrations. Within his political intervention framework, he has proposed lowering the voting age limit to 16 and changes to university access systems. From a different political starting point, Marine Le Pen has advocated strengthening police powers against violent protesters, while Édouard Philippe has condemned attacks and destruction. In this manner, the same social event transforms into a field of confrontation among differing political perceptions on public education, security, and the role of the state. Can students influence the ballot box? Interestingly, many current students lack voting rights as yet. Nevertheless, mobilizations can influence political debate in three ways. First, they bring the state of education to the center of the pre-electoral agenda, forcing candidates to present concrete proposals. Second, they can mobilize families, educators, and older youth who already hold voting rights. Third, they highlight differing perceptions on police management of social mobilizations. Electoral impact, however, is not given. In the 2022 presidential elections, according to data cited by Le Monde , Jean-Luc Mélenchon gathered 36% among voters aged 18–24, but turnout for this age group reached only 52%. This example shows why massive youth presence in the streets does not automatically translate into corresponding electoral turnout or support for a specific candidate. Albania: Edi Rama facing demands for early elections In Albania, the electoral dimension differs. Edi Rama secured a fourth consecutive election victory in 2025, while the next scheduled parliamentary elections are projected for 2029. Consequently, no immediate scheduled national electoral contest comparable to France's exists. However, the opposition Democratic Party has expressed support for demonstrations and demands forming a caretaker government aiming to hold early elections . Edi Rama rejects the resignation demand and insists governments change through the democratic electoral process. Here lies the core political confrontation: protesters demanding government change seek immediate developments, whereas the government invokes the popular mandate received just the previous year. Mobilizations can increase political pressure, but do not automatically entail early elections. Such an outcome would require specific political and institutional developments. The deeper crisis: A generation no longer trusting promises Behind the images of incidents lies a social issue unexplained solely through partisan confrontation. In France, students describe schools with staff shortages, overly demanding curricula, and infrastructure problems. In Albania, youth speak of expensive studies, career placement difficulties, and a political environment where they feel unrepresented. The two societies differ significantly regarding economic status, educational systems, and institutions. Yet the sense of uncertainty regarding the future appears in both cases. Education traditionally links with the promise of social progress. When youth consider this promise unfulfilled, discontent can transform into political challenge. This does not mean all demonstrators hold identical views or seek political system overthrow; rather, specific educational problems can serve as a springboard for broader social mobilization. The risk of escalation — When protest meets violence Developments in France and Albania also highlight a significant risk. As tension mounts, initial demands increasingly risk being overshadowed by clash imagery. In France, the ACLED organization recorded over 800 student demonstrations solely between September 28 and October 2. Concurrently, it reports severe destruction and police violence incidents, including heavy student injuries. In Albania, attacks on public buildings and police led to even more intense confrontations regarding protest limits and state reaction. Condemnation of violence against individuals and infrastructure does not negate the need to examine social causes behind mobilizations. Correspondingly, justified demands do not render attacks acceptable. https://www.dw.com/en/myanmar-is-us-unde.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ok7r Prefer DW on Google The head of Myanmar's junta, Min Aung Hlaing, became the head of the country's nominally civilian government in April 2026 Image: Aung Shine Oo/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement The US government has begun a quiet reproachment with Myanmar 's military-backed government, holding two rounds of talks since September with State Department representative Michael Vance. American diplomats reportedly meet Myanmar officials in Naypyitaw and then in Tokyo earlier this month. Washington wants to tackle online scam centers, secure the release of imprisoned American businessman Adam Castillo, and potentially gain access to Myanmar's rare-earth resources . The market for the valuable minerals is currently controlled by the US rival China . Meanwhile, Southeast Asian governments are also increasingly questioning their policy of isolating Myanmar's military leadership. Multiple countries have already renewed direct diplomatic contacts. The EU, however, continues to reject the legitimacy of the military junta in the war-torn country. The European bloc has also remained unmoved by the 2025/2026 election , which ended with military chief Min Aung Hlaing becoming the president . The military retains control over the political system. Human Rights Watch's Elaine Pearson on Myanmar election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video EU's sanctions still in force The EU responded to Myanmar's February 2021 military coup by suspending direct financial assistance to the government, imposing targeted sanctions and sharply reducing diplomatic engagement with the military authorities. Despite the Western boycott, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing has made official trips to India, China and Russia [FILE: June 1, 2026] Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance Its sanctions currently cover 105 individuals and 22 entities connected to the military. In April, the EU extended these measures for another 12 months. At the same time, Brussels is providing humanitarian assistance to displaced communities and Rohingya refugees and is supporting civil society organizations. Thailand-Myanmar border clinic helps people fleeing war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EU also stopped short of withdrawing Myanmar's preferential trade access because of concerns about the consequences for workers, particularly the mostly young women employed in the country's garment industry. Last year, bilateral goods trade was worth about €4 billion ($4.46 billion), up from €3.4 billion in 2019. Brussels supports ASEAN's peace deal The civil war triggered by the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people. Rebel groups still control or contest large swathes of Myanmar, and over 4 million people have been internally displaced, according to UN data. The EU "continues to uphold its policy of non-recognition of the current military regime," in view of "the ongoing violence and the attack against its own population," an EU spokesman told DW. At the same time, the bloc "is closely monitoring developments in the discussions and positions of the United States, Japan, ASEAN countries and other major actors with representatives of Myanmar's military regime." "It also supports ASEAN efforts, in particular the Five-Point Consensus, which has yet to be fully implemented," the spokesperson added, referring to the peace deal proposed by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2021. Myanmar diplomats reach out to European partners In the aftermath of the coup, ASEAN took the unprecedented decision to exclude Myanmar's military leaders from its highest-level meetings after the junta failed to implement the regional peace plan. However, ASEAN's position is showing signs of change. Some member states, most notably Myanmar's neighbor Thailand , signal growing frustration with the lack of progress towards ending Myanmar's civil war. New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Last week, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow welcomed Washington's renewed engagement and suggested that ASEAN members would hold substantive discussions about Myanmar's future at their summit in Manila next month. Myanmar's authorities are also seeking to break their diplomatic isolation . In September, Myanmar's leader Hlaing gave an interview to Time magazine, his first with a major Western publication since the coup, as part of an apparent effort to rebuild relations with Western governments. On October 22, Burma Campaign UK, a London-based human rights organization, accused the British government of making a "significant shift in approach" after the British Foreign Office hosted Win Zeyar Tun, the charge d'affaires of Myanmar's military-controlled embassy in London, at an ASEAN diplomatic gathering days earlier. According to an article published by Intelligence Online this month, the regime's charge d'affaires in Brussels, Khin Thidar Ay, has also sought contacts with European politicians, including Czech MEP Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament's delegation for Southeast Asia. EU's isolation 'has achieved relatively little' Kristina Kironska, of Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic and an expert on the EU's policy on Myanmar, told DW that the EU has little reason to follow Washington's apparent shift towards engagement with the Myanmar junta. The US strategy "appears to be pursuing specific interests" such as rare earth mining and cybercrime, she said. "It remains to be seen what the US can achieve through negotiations with the junta," she said. The EU has long positioned itself as a defender of democracy and human rights in Myanmar, "so abandoning this now because the US is exploring a new, perhaps more transactional approach would undermine the EU's credibility," Kironska added. "At the same time, isolation has achieved relatively little. The question is therefore not whether the EU should engage, but rather with whom and under what conditions." Balancing act between Myanmar's rebels and junta The EU is forced to consider risks to its own influence. If Washington, ASEAN governments and other regional powers increase their engagement with Myanmar's authorities , the EU risks becoming increasingly marginal in discussions about the country's political future. Yet greater engagement with the military could undermine Brussels' relations with Myanmar's democratic opposition and ethnic resistance organizations, many of which control substantial territory. "The key question for Brussels is whether it can remain a credible defender of democratic change while ensuring that it still has a meaningful voice in the negotiations that will determine Myanmar's future ," Sabe Soe, director of the NGO Burma Centre Prague, told DW. One possibility is for Brussels to maintain its sanctions against military leaders and their businesses while expanding diplomacy through ASEAN, the UN and other regional partners. The EU could also tie any easing of restrictions to humanitarian access, improvements in political freedoms and progress towards peace. Soe also suggested that the EU could pursue economic engagement in areas administered by revolutionary and ethnic resistance forces, offering an alternative to engagement centered on the military authorities in Naypyidaw. This approach would allow the EU to remain involved in Myanmar's future without necessarily recognizing its military-backed government, she said. For now, Brussels seems to have little appetite for a fundamental policy rethink. But this could change as more governments reopen their doors to Myanmar's generals.
